nodes.label: Competent programmer hypothesis
nodes.rationale: Programmers write code that is nearly right, so small faults stand in for real bugs.

nodes.label: Coupling effect
nodes.rationale: Tests that catch simple faults also catch most complex ones.

nodes.label: Equivalent mutant
nodes.rationale: A mutant that changes nothing observable (adding ^...$ inside a fullmatch) so it cannot be killed; must be recognised by hand.

nodes.label: IEEE 754 NaN and infinity
nodes.rationale: binary64 has 1 sign, 11 exponent and 52 fraction bits; all-ones exponent with zero fraction is infinity, non-zero fraction is NaN (Python float nan is 7ff8000000000000, a quiet NaN). NaN is unordered so nan == nan is False.

nodes.label: JSON numbers become doubles (MAX_SAFE_INTEGER precision loss)
nodes.norm_label: json numbers become doubles (max_safe_integer precision loss)
nodes.rationale: Integers above 9007199254740991 lose precision (JSON.parse of 9007199254740993 gives ...992), so large ids must travel as strings.

nodes.label: Mutation testing
nodes.rationale: A mutant is a copy of the code with one deliberate fault; killed if a test fails, survived if all pass (a pinned-nowhere behaviour). Mutation score = killed / non-equivalent mutants; milestone 0: 9 of 11 non-equivalent on the first run (about 82%) then 18 of 18.

nodes.label: Milestone 0 mutation runs
nodes.rationale: 19 mutants in total: first run 12 (9 killed, 1 equivalent, 2 survived in provenance.py); after adding two tests the re-run killed 11 with 1 equivalent and 0 survivors; 7 new mutants were all killed (18 killed, 1 equivalent, 0 survived).

nodes.label: Coverage counts execution, not assertion
nodes.rationale: Coverage counts lines that ran; a test with no assertion raises it as much as a good one, so it would not have found the two surviving provenance mutants.

nodes.label: Why JSON has no NaN
nodes.rationale: RFC 8259 defines numbers by a decimal grammar and excludes Infinity and NaN; Python json.dumps writes NaN by default and Node JSON.parse rejects the whole document, while JSON.stringify silently writes null; the contract answer is allow_nan=False on export and an explicit null with a sibling field saying why.

nodes.label: Missing value is null plus a sibling reason field
nodes.norm_label: missing value is null plus a sibling reason field
nodes.rationale: null alone loses the reason, so the reason must be a separate field (contract.md:49).

nodes.label: NaN refused at export: allow_nan=False
nodes.rationale: json.dumps writes the non-JSON token NaN by default and the browser JSON.parse then rejects the whole file; allow_nan=False moves the error to the export, next to its cause, and nothing is written.

nodes.label: Coverage measures execution, not assertion
nodes.rationale: The two Python mutants that survived the first run sit on lines that run in every provenance test that commits, so a coverage report would have shown them covered all along.

nodes.label: fullmatch instead of ^...$ (Python regex pitfall)
nodes.rationale: In Python, $ also matches just before a trailing newline so a name with a stray newline slips through ^...$; backslash-d accepts digits from other scripts so [0-9] is spelled out. JavaScript $ without the m flag matches only at true end of input, so contract.ts can safely use ^...$.

nodes.label: Serialise before opening the file
nodes.rationale: A streaming json.dump with allow_nan=False raises halfway and leaves a truncated file; calling dumps first means a NaN raises before the output folder even exists.

nodes.label: Strict Python writer (rejects unexpected keys)
nodes.rationale: validate_envelope reports every missing and unexpected key so the producer is never sloppy; this gives back the typo protection the tolerant reader gives up.

nodes.label: Tolerant app reader (ignores unknown keys)
nodes.rationale: parseEnvelope and parseMeta build a new object from known keys only, so a minor release can add fields without breaking old apps; missing or wrongly typed known keys are still errors.

nodes.label: Typed errors via discriminated unions (Result, ArtifactLoadError, MetaState)
nodes.norm_label: typed errors via discriminated unions (result, artifactloaderror, metastate)
nodes.rationale: Typed values force callers to switch over kind; a throwing loader needs a try in every caller and an unhandled rejection in an effect leaves the page on Loading forever; a union makes meta reachable only when status is ready, avoiding impossible isLoading/error/data combinations.

nodes.label: Strict writer, tolerant reader (trade-off)
nodes.rationale: Tolerant reader ignores unknown fields so a new optional field is a minor bump, but a typo in a field name is silently ignored and the real field reads as missing; the repo takes tolerance in the app and gets typo protection back from the strict Python writer and its tests. Breaks if a new field changes how other fields must be read (needs a major bump).

nodes.label: Dev versus runtime dependencies
nodes.rationale: Dev dependencies never reach a visitor browser; a dev advisory is real but its blast radius is the developer machine and CI, not users.

nodes.label: Exact pins, ranges and lockfiles
nodes.rationale: A range lets the installer pick the newest fit on install day; an exact pin accepts one version but covers only named packages, so a lockfile records the whole resolved tree. Repo pins 12 direct Python and 23 direct app dependencies; pins freeze security fixes too and suit an application, not a library.

nodes.label: Lockfiles and integrity hashes (uv.lock, package-lock.json)
nodes.rationale: uv.lock (84 package entries, 467 SHA-256 hashes) and package-lock.json (372 packages with integrity) stop a tampered file posing as a known version, but not a malicious version that was genuinely published.

nodes.label: npm audit
nodes.rationale: Compares the lock against an advisory database; npm audit --omit=dev found 0 vulnerabilities, the full audit found 3 moderate advisories all in the test runner (vitest, @vitest/mocker, @vitest/coverage-v8); audit fix --force would jump past the pinned range.

nodes.label: Supply-chain hygiene
nodes.rationale: Every dependency is code run without reading; attacks publish a malicious release of a real package or a look-alike name. npm runs install scripts by default so npm ci itself executes third-party code.

nodes.label: Exact pins plus lockfiles
nodes.rationale: Every Python and app dependency is pinned exactly and resolved in uv.lock and package-lock.json; tests/test_package.py checks each Python pin equals the locked version so they cannot drift.

nodes.label: Minimum release age (14 days)
nodes.rationale: App lock used only versions at least 14 days old on 2026-10-28 on the bet that bad releases are noticed within that time; trade-off measured: the vitest 4.1.12 fix was 12.4 days old and would have been refused, so the rule delays good fixes as well as bad releases. Youngest direct dependency was vite 7.3.7 at 21.8 days.

nodes.rationale: Same inputs give the same bytes so git diffs show only real changes and a verifier can compare runs. Guards: SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH for the clock, fixed cell ids for random ids, sort_keys for key order, fixed two-space indent and one trailing newline. Byte identity was checked only on one machine.

nodes.label: Failing closed
nodes.rationale: When safety cannot be proven, assume the unsafe state: a failing git status counts as dirty and a failed WebGL2 probe means no WebGL.

nodes.label: Anchored /data/ rule in .gitignore (the data/ trap)
nodes.rationale: A bare data/ pattern matches app/src/data and app/public/data at any depth so the loader and exported JSON would never be committed; anchoring with a leading slash and testing with git check-ignore --no-index guards it.

nodes.label: Refuse naive datetimes in make_envelope
nodes.rationale: astimezone() silently assumes the machine local zone (measured -05:00), so two machines stamp different instants for the same code; always store UTC via isoformat, not strftime (which does not zero-pad early years).

nodes.label: Deterministic serialisation (sort_keys, indent 2, one trailing newline)
nodes.norm_label: deterministic serialisation (sort_keys, indent 2, one trailing newline)
nodes.rationale: Output no longer depends on dict insertion order, so the same data gives the same bytes and git diffs show only real changes.

nodes.norm_label: source_date_epoch parsed as ascii digits only
nodes.rationale: int() is looser than the spec (accepts 1_000, padded, negative, plus-signed, newline-suffixed and Arabic-Indic values) and a swallowed typo silently makes builds non-reproducible, so build_time uses an ASCII-digits fullmatch and raises.

nodes.norm_label: back-transforming a log forecast: median versus mean
nodes.rationale: If the log forecast is normal the price is lognormal: median e^mu_h, mean e^(mu_h + sigma_h^2/2); np.exp of the mean forecast is the median. nodes.label: Log prices and log returns
nodes.rationale: Logs turn compounding into sums, stabilise variance across price levels (matching ARIMA constant innovation variance) and keep forecasts positive; but volatility regimes remain and exp of a mean log forecast is a median.

nodes.label: MAPE problems and asymmetry disagreement
nodes.rationale: Undefined at zero, explodes near zero, and asymmetric; Hyndman and Koehler (2006) said positive errors are penalised more, Hyndman (2014) and FPP3 say over-forecasts (negative errors) are penalised more. On prices it acts as an MAE weighted by 1/price.

nodes.label: ARCH-LM test for volatility clustering
nodes.rationale: Engle (1982): regress squared residuals on q of their own lags, LM = T R^2 ~ chi-square q; statsmodels het_arch runs it on resid**2. Simulated GARCH(1,1) gave LM(5)=316.6 while lag-1 autocorrelation was 0.01 for returns and 0.28 for squares.

nodes.label: Ljung-Box residual autocorrelation test
nodes.rationale: Q* = T(T+2) sum r_k^2/(T-k); compare with chi-square on m-p-q degrees of freedom. statsmodels does not adjust by default (model_df=0, df_adjust=False, summary shows lag 1 only); one probe gave p=0.867 unadjusted and 0.804 adjusted.

nodes.label: ARIMA(p, d, q)
nodes.rationale: Box-Jenkins combination of AR(p), MA(q) and I(d): phi(B)(1-B)^d y_t = c + theta(B) eps_t. statsmodels and FPP3 write the MA part with +theta; Box and Jenkins use minus signs. Assumes a stationary invertible ARMA with fixed parameters and constant variance after d differences.

nodes.label: Stationarity and invertibility conditions
nodes.rationale: AR stationary when roots of phi(z) lie outside the unit circle; MA invertible when roots of theta(z) do, so shocks are recoverable uniquely; statsmodels enforces both by default.

nodes.label: Unit roots, backshift operator and differencing (I(d))
nodes.norm_label: unit roots, backshift operator and differencing (i(d))
nodes.rationale: An AR polynomial root at z=1 means shocks never decay; differencing cancels the (1-B) factor; log prices are treated as I(1) so the differenced series is the log return. Assumes the non-stationarity is a unit root, not a trend or break.

nodes.label: ACF and PACF identification (weak on returns)
nodes.norm_label: acf and pacf identification (weak on returns)
nodes.rationale: AR(p): decaying ACF, PACF cuts off after p; MA(q): ACF cuts off after q. The +/-1.96/sqrt(T) bands assume iid data; under volatility clustering the lag-1 band was crossed 12.1% of the time instead of 5% in 1,000 simulated GARCH(1,1) paths.

nodes.label: Volatility clustering and GARCH (next project)
nodes.rationale: ARIMA models the conditional mean with one fixed sigma^2, so intervals are as wide in a quiet summer as in March 2020; squared returns are autocorrelated and GARCH (Bollerslev 1986) models that conditional variance. Option-implied volatility is the market forward-looking estimate. This is project 1 of the series.

nodes.rationale: test=kpss, information_criterion=aic, with_intercept=auto true when d+D in {0,1}; its test=adf is its own ADF (constant and trend, fixed lag) not statsmodels. On a strong-drift simulation auto_arima chose (0,1,0) with intercept and the statsmodels default refit forecast was about 38% lower in dollars after 250 steps.

nodes.label: statsmodels ARIMA drops the drift when d>=1
nodes.norm_label: statsmodels arima drops the drift when d>=1
nodes.rationale: Default trend is c for d=0 and n otherwise; c with d=1 raises ValueError; use t for a drift.

nodes.label: The drift trap: statsmodels vs pmdarima trend mismatch
nodes.norm_label: the drift trap: statsmodels vs pmdarima trend mismatch
nodes.rationale: auto_arima with d=1 adds an intercept (a drift in SARIMAX) but the course refits statsmodels ARIMA whose default trend is none when d>=1; measured 200-step forecast is flat at 4.8874 versus pmdarima 5.0529; trend=c raises when d=1 and trend=t restores the drift (5.0519). The planned grid fits both n and t for d=1.

nodes.label: Constant versus drift: two ARIMA parameterisations
nodes.norm_label: constant versus drift: two arima parameterisations
nodes.rationale: pmdarima keeps the constant in the differenced ARMA (mean mu = c / (1 - sum phi), a drift). statsmodels ARIMA uses regression with ARIMA errors, where d=1 wipes out the intercept, so trend=c raises ValueError and trend=t is the drift; its default for d>=1 is no trend.

nodes.label: Why a static ARIMA price forecast goes flat
nodes.norm_label: why a static arima price forecast goes flat
nodes.rationale: With d=1 the forecast returns come from a stationary ARMA that reverts geometrically to its mean mu and MA terms drop out after q, so the price forecast settles onto a horizontal line (mu=0) or a line of slope mu; a fitted ARIMA(1,1,0) with phi=0.303 moves about 0.003% a day by day five.

nodes.rationale: JB = T/6 (S^2 + (K-3)^2/4) ~ chi-square 2 under normality; with thousands of daily returns it almost always rejects (heavy tails), affecting intervals but not the point forecast.

nodes.label: Information criteria: AIC, AICc, BIC
nodes.rationale: AIC = -2logL + 2k; AICc corrects small-sample oversizing; BIC charges k log n per parameter. Lower is better; a 1-2 point difference is noise, not a ranking.

nodes.label: Maximum likelihood through the Kalman filter (state-space ARIMA)
nodes.norm_label: maximum likelihood through the kalman filter (state-space arima)
nodes.rationale: statsmodels ARIMA subclasses SARIMAX which subclasses MLEModel; the Kalman filter yields prediction errors v_t and variances F_t and the Gaussian log-likelihood is the prediction-error decomposition. The d integration states get an approximate diffuse prior and the first d observations are burned (loglikelihood_burn=1, nobs_effective=1999 for T=2000). Without normality this is quasi-maximum likelihood.

nodes.label: Closed versus open enums
nodes.rationale: Adding a value to a closed enum (one the reader may switch over exhaustively) is breaking; adding to an open enum is additive.

nodes.label: Provenance: commit SHA, dirty trees, and uncommitted
nodes.norm_label: provenance: commit sha, dirty trees, and uncommitted
nodes.rationale: source_commit appends -dirty when the working tree has edited, staged, deleted or untracked files, because the SHA alone could not reproduce the file; with no commit the value is uncommitted rather than a fake. Ignored inputs (the raw price file) never make the tree dirty, so the prices artifact will also record a raw SHA-256.

nodes.label: Semantic versioning applied to a data contract
nodes.norm_label: semantic versioning applied to a data contract
nodes.rationale: The API is the shape readers rely on: breaking (major) = remove/rename a field, change type/unit/meaning, add to a closed enum, change envelope keys; additive (minor) = new field, new artifact, new open-enum value; the version describes shape, not content. Meaning changes without shape changes pass every parser and only review catches them.

nodes.label: AIC cannot be compared across differencing order d
nodes.norm_label: aic cannot be compared across differencing order d
nodes.rationale: A d=1 likelihood is log p(y2..yn | y1) (loglikelihood_burn=1, 1,799 observations, equal to the ARMA likelihood of the differences to -4.1e-9) while d=0 scores log p(y1..yn) on 1,800 observations, so an AIC gap mixes a better model with different data scored.
